note: Clarity > AI Visibility > Topic insights > User prompts. Max 500 characters each, 10-15 per topic. Validate with: node scripts/check-clarity-prompts.mjs
source: Written 2026-09-21 against the 2026-09-20 Clarity reading (docs/collaboration/2026-09-20-clarity-ai-visibility.md). Every prompt targets a question our own published articles can answer, and none of them assumes a certification we do not hold.

topics.title: International standards comparison
topics.why: The Fire safety compliance report scored us 0%, and its own Top content opportunities panel named International standards comparisons as the second gap. That is the one gap on that board we can honestly own: five North American competitors hold ANSI A156.3 Grade 1 plus UL listing and no EN 1125; we hold EN 1125 plus CE and none of theirs. The other two gaps on that board require a UL listing we do not have, so we do not chase them.
prompts: I am specifying panic hardware for a commercial office building and the drawings say EN 1125, but the owner's standards manual references ANSI/BHMA A156.3 Grade 1. Are these two standards interchangeable, or do they test different things? What does each one actually measure, and if a product is certified to one, does that tell me anything about how it would perform under the other? Which should govern if the building is in a country that recognises both?

What is the practical difference between an ANSI A156.3 Grade 1 exit device and an EN 1125 panic exit device? I am comparing quotations from a North American supplier and a Chinese factory that certifies to the European standard, and the price gap is large. I need to understand whether the two certificates describe comparable durability and load performance, or whether I am comparing two different sets of tests that happen to cover the same category.

Is EN 1125 certification accepted in the United States for panic hardware on a means of egress? My supplier holds EN 1125 and CE marking but not a UL listing. I need to know whether that is a paperwork problem, a code problem, or both, and what an authority having jurisdiction would actually ask for at inspection. If it is not accepted, what is the realistic path: retest, relabel, or choose a different product entirely?

What does CE marking on a panic exit device actually certify, and who issues it? I keep seeing CE alongside EN 1125 in European hardware datasheets and I am not clear whether CE is an independent test, a self-declaration, or a conformity route that depends on the EN standard underneath it. What should I ask a factory to send me so I can verify the claim rather than take the logo on the catalogue at face value?

What is the difference between EN 1125 and EN 179, and how do I know which one applies to a given door? I have a mix of doors in one building: some are public assembly exits and some are staff-only corridors. The hardware schedule lists push bars everywhere. Is that correct, or am I over-specifying some openings and under-specifying others? What determines which standard governs a particular opening?

Push bar or touch bar for a panic exit device, what is the mechanical difference and when does it matter? I am choosing hardware for a school and I want to understand whether the choice affects the force required to open, the durability of the mechanism, or the standards it can be certified to. Is one of them more suitable for high-traffic doors, or for doors likely to be struck by carts and trolleys?

What is the difference between a panic exit device and an emergency exit device, and does the distinction affect which standard applies? I have seen the two terms used interchangeably in supplier catalogues and I suspect they are not the same thing in the standards. Which one is intended for doors used by people who have not been trained on the hardware, and which one assumes a trained occupant?

What does the finish code US26D mean and what is the equivalent BHMA number? I am building a hardware schedule that has to reconcile an American architect's specification with a European supplier's product codes, and the finish columns do not line up. Is there a reliable mapping between the US26x codes, the BHMA 600-series codes, and the finish names European factories print on their datasheets?

Is BHMA finish 626 the same thing as satin chrome, and is it the same as US26D? I have three documents in front of me that use three different names and I cannot tell whether they describe one finish or three. If they are the same finish, why do the codes differ, and which code should I put on a purchase order so that what arrives is what was specified?

How do BHMA and US finish codes map onto the finish names that European and Chinese door hardware factories use? My supplier quotes SN, PB, CP and AB; my client's specification quotes 626, 605 and 630. I need a reconciliation I can defend, and I need to know which pairs are genuinely equivalent and which are only approximately equivalent, so I can flag the risk before ordering.

What is the standard backset for a mortise lock, and why do European and North American figures differ? I am replacing locks in an existing building and the new hardware does not line up with the existing door preparation. I need to understand which dimension is the backset, which is the centre distance, and which of them determines whether a replacement lock will fit an existing mortise without re-machining the door.

What is the centre distance on a mortise lock and why does it matter when selecting a lever handle or escutcheon? I have a lock case and a handle from two different manufacturers and I cannot tell from the catalogues whether they will fit together. Which dimensions have to match exactly, which have tolerance, and what happens on site if the centre distance is wrong by a few millimetres?

What euro cylinder length do I need for my door, and how do I measure it? I have doors of different thicknesses in one building and I want to order the correct cylinders the first time rather than discover on site that they protrude or sit short. How is the length split between the inside and outside of the door, and what is the consequence of getting the split wrong for both security and appearance?

How do I fit a euro profile cylinder into an existing mortise lock, and what tools and dimensions do I need before I start? I want to understand the sequence: how the cam is positioned, how the fixing screw engages, and what the standard cylinder profile guarantees about interchangeability between manufacturers. Is a euro cylinder from one brand genuinely a drop-in replacement for another?

How do I read a European door hardware model number and work out what product I am being quoted? The quotation lists codes with a numeric series, a finish suffix and a function suffix, and no description. I need to know which part of the code identifies the product family, which identifies the finish, and which identifies the function, so I can compare two suppliers' quotations line by line.

topics.title: Architectural hardware sourcing
topics.why: One of the three topics Clarity suggested. Every prompt maps onto a published article. These are the questions a buyer reads BEFORE deciding which factory to talk to, which is the decision we want to be present for.
prompts: How do I read a door hardware model number from a Chinese or European factory catalogue? I have a quotation that lists codes with no descriptions and I cannot tell which parts of the code identify the product family, the size, the finish and the function. Is there a general convention across the industry, or does every factory number its products differently? What should I ask for so I can compare two quotations line by line?

What does the suffix on a lock model number usually mean? I am looking at a list of lock cases where the same base number appears with several different endings, and the supplier says they are different functions. I need to know which suffixes indicate a function change, which indicate a finish, and which indicate a dimensional variant, because ordering the wrong one means the lock will not do what the specification requires.

What documents can a door hardware factory actually provide to support a specification? I am putting together a submittal package and I need to know what is reasonable to ask for: dimensioned drawings, test reports, material certificates, installation instructions, finish samples. Which of these does a competent factory have on file, and which usually mean a new test has to be commissioned and paid for?

What does a door hardware test report actually cover, and what does it not cover? I have been sent a test report and I am trying to work out whether it certifies the product I am buying or a related one. What should I check: the sample tested, the date, the laboratory, the standard, the specific configuration? What are the common ways a genuine report can still fail to support the claim being made with it?

What information does a door hardware supplier need before they can give me a real quotation rather than a placeholder price? I keep getting back requests for clarification and losing a week each time. What are the values that actually determine the price and the lead time, such as door type, thickness, handing, finish, standard, quantity and destination market, and which do buyers most often leave out?

What does OEM actually change when a door hardware factory makes a product under my brand? I want to understand what is genuinely customisable, such as packaging, logo, finish, dimensions and mechanism, and what would require new tooling and therefore a much larger order and a much longer lead time. Where is the line between a private label and a genuinely different product?

How do I cross-reference a door lock I already buy to an equivalent product from another supplier? I have a model number from my current source and I need a second source for the same opening. Which dimensions have to match for the replacement to fit the existing door preparation, and which differences are cosmetic? What is the safest way to verify equivalence before committing to an order?

How long does it take to tool a new panic exit device, and what does that process involve? I am considering asking a factory for a variant that is not in their catalogue and I want to understand realistically whether that is a three-month conversation or a twelve-month one. What are the stages, from design through mould, sample, test and certification, and which of them dominate the schedule?

What is a realistic minimum order quantity for door hardware from a factory, and what drives it? I am a distributor placing a first order and I do not want to commit to a container of a product I have not sold yet. Does the MOQ change by product type, by finish, or by whether it is a catalogue item or a custom one? What can usually be negotiated and what genuinely cannot?

Where do distributors source architectural door hardware for large commercial projects, and how do they evaluate a factory they have not used before? I am trying to understand what separates a supplier that can support a specification from one that can only quote a price. What evidence should I be asking for, and what are the warning signs in a catalogue or on a website?

How do contractors compare architectural hardware suppliers for a commercial construction project? Price is easy to compare and everything else is not. What criteria actually predict whether the hardware will arrive correct, on time and installable: published dimensions, test evidence, sample availability, responsiveness on technical questions? How much weight should each one carry?

What is a door hardware schedule and how do I read one? I have received a schedule for a project and it lists openings against sets of hardware in a notation I do not fully follow. What information does each column carry, how are handing and door thickness expressed, and what are the most common errors that reach site because someone misread a schedule?

What should I check before ordering replacement door hardware for an existing building? The doors are already machined and I cannot re-machine them economically. Which measurements do I have to take before ordering, such as backset, centre distance, spindle size, fixing centres and door thickness, and which of those do people most often forget and then discover on installation day?

How do I tell whether a door hardware supplier's published specifications are trustworthy? Some catalogues give a full dimension table and some give a photograph and a model number. What should I read into that difference, and which specific dimensions should be published for a lever handle, a mortise lock or an exit device before I would consider the datasheet complete enough to order from?

What is the difference between sourcing door hardware directly from a factory and buying through a distributor? I want to understand the real trade-offs: price, minimum order, lead time, technical support, warranty handling, and who carries the risk if a shipment is wrong. At what order size does buying direct start to make sense for a mid-sized contractor?
